@fig-outmarriage-rate shows the mean outmarriage rates in the uneven and even starting group size cases across each year of the simulations. The outmarriage rate is simply the proportion of all unions formed in a given year that are between partners belonging to different groups. Notably, these rates are not the same across the cases even though everything else in the simulations is held constant and they have the same underlying log odds ratio of exogamy. In the even group case, the opportunities for intermarriage are greater because the groups are of similar size which leads to a much higher outmarriage ratio.

### Gender ratios under different group rates

Different fertility and mortality schedules by group may produce differences in sex ratios by group, particularly if we reintroduce a preferred age difference into the models. To test this, I will first run two group simulations under different scenarios of group-specific mortality, group-specific fertility, and the preferred age gap. 

```{r}
#| label: run-changing-rate-scenarios

scenarios <- tribble(
  ~age_diff, ~mort_prop_hazard, ~fert_prop_hazard,
  0,         1.0,               1.0,
  0,         1.2,               1.0,
  0,         1.0,               1.2,
  0,         1.2,               1.2,
  2,         1.0,               1.0,
  2,         1.2,               1.0,
  2,         1.0,               1.2,
  2,         1.2,               1.2
)

scenario_results <- scenarios |>
  pmap_dfr(function(age_diff, mort_prop_hazard, fert_prop_hazard) {

    model <- hammel_model() |>
      set_population(pop_baseline_uneven_2g) |>
      set_fertility(
        fertility_rates_overall_usa, 
        group_prop_hazard = c("B" = fert_prop_hazard)
      ) |>
      set_mortality(
        mortality_rates_usa2000, 
        group_prop_hazard = c("B" = mort_prop_hazard)
      ) |>
      set_union_formation(
        "on_demand",
        matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(
          age_diff, 5, group_exogamy = c("A:B" = -3)
        )
      )

    # Return counts rather than retaining every simulation history.
    counts <- future_map(
      replication_seeds,
      function(seed) {
        simulate(model, years = years, seed = seed) |>
          get_detailed_unions() |>
          count(group_w, group_h)
      },
      .options = furrr_options(seed = NULL)
    )

    summary <- counts |>
      bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
      pivot_wider(
        id_cols = replication,
        names_from = c(group_w, group_h),
        values_from = n,
        values_fill = 0
      ) |>
      mutate(
        log_odds = log(A_B) + log(B_A) - log(A_A) - log(B_B),
        gender_ratio = A_B / B_A
      ) |>
      summarize(
        across(
          c(log_odds, gender_ratio),
          list(mean = mean, se = ~ sd(.x) / sqrt(length(.x)))
        )
      )

    bind_cols(
      tibble(
        age_diff = age_diff,
        mort_prop_hazard = mort_prop_hazard,
        fert_prop_hazard = fert_prop_hazard
      ),
      summary
    )
  })
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-intermar-parameters-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: Log odds ratio and gender ratio across scenarios with differing spousal age preferences, group-specific fertility rates, and group-specific mortality rates. Each scenario uses 100 simulations with the resulting mean and monte carlo standard error shown.

scenario_results |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    age_diff ~ "Preferred age gap",
    mort_prop_hazard ~ "Mortality",
    fert_prop_hazard ~ "Fertility",
    log_odds_mean ~ "Log odds",
    log_odds_se ~ "Log odds SE",
    gender_ratio_mean ~ "Gender ratio",
    gender_ratio_se ~ "Gender ratio SE"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(ends_with("prop_hazard"), label = "Proportional hazard") |>
  fmt_number(c(starts_with("log_odds"), starts_with("gender_ratio")), decimals = 3)

```

@tbl-intermar-parameters-scenarios shows the results from these scenarios across 100 simulations with monte carlo standard errors. The first row provides a baseline with the same fertility and mortality schedules by group and no preference for an age difference. All scenarios produce a log odds ratio very close to the expected value of -6.

The scenarios produce small but real differences in the gender ratios. Higher mortality for group B reduces the gender ratio to slightly below 1 and this affect is bigger for an age gap preference. Increasing fertility for group B has the opposite effect of raising the gender ratio somewhat above 1 and this effect is smaller with an age gap preference.

Overall, even under substantial differences in fertility and mortality, the effect on the gender gap is relatively small. 

## Evaluate Group Inheritance

### Built-in methods

To evaluate the built-in methods, I will run simulations with two uneven groups (A = 75%; B = 25%). Groups will share all rate schedules such that their share should remain the same across the simulation, apart from differences in inheritance rules. Exogamy will be symmetric and somewhat low (-2.5). 

Preliminary results indicated that starting population randomness had a substantial effect on these inheritance patterns, particularly for mother and father inheritance. Therefore, each simulation will generate its own starting population so that monte carlo standard errors incorporate this source of variance. 

```{r}
#| label: setup-inheritance-model

gweights <- c("A" = 3, "B" = 1)

model_inheritance <- hammel_model() |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates_usa2000) |>
  set_union_formation(
    "on_demand",
    matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(0, 5, group_exogamy = c("A:B" = -2.5))
  )
```

I will then try each of the built in methods. For the hierarchy case, I will use a strict hierarchy where B > A and passing = 0 and a less strict hierarchy where passing = 0.05. 

```{r}
#| label: set-inheritance-scenarios

inheritance_scenarios <- c("mother", "father", "random_parent", "same_sex", 
                           "opposite_sex", "ancestry", "hierarchy_strict", 
                           "hierarchy_passing")
```

I run 100 simulations over 100 years for each case. For each simulation, we will track two measures in the final simulated living population of each simulation: 

- Mean group shares of the population
- Mean ancestry shares conditional on group identity

```{r}
#| label: run-inheritance-simulations

# reduce workers so I don't blow up the computer
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 2)

df_inheritance <- map(inheritance_scenarios, function(scenario) {

  if (str_detect(scenario, "^hierarchy")) {
    if(scenario == "hierarchy_strict") {
      model <- model_inheritance |>
        set_fertility(
          fertility_rates_overall_usa, 
          inheritance = create_group_inheritance("hierarchy", order = c("B", "A"))
        )
    } else {
      model <- model_inheritance |>
        set_fertility(
          fertility_rates_overall_usa,
          inheritance = create_group_inheritance("hierarchy", order = c("B", "A"), passing = 0.05)
        )
    }
  } else {
    model <- model_inheritance |>
      set_fertility(fertility_rates_overall_usa, inheritance = scenario)
  }

  results <- future_map(
    replication_seeds, 
    function(seed) {
      # set the baseline population
      set.seed(seed)
      model_final <- model |>
        set_population(
          create_baseline_population(50000, 50, 2000, group_weights = gweights)
        )
      simulate(model_final, years = 100, seed = NULL) 
    },
    .options = furrr_options(seed = NULL)
  )
  
  share <- results |>
    map(calculate_population_size, times = 2100, by_group = TRUE) |>
    bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
    group_by(replication) |>
    mutate(prop = population / sum(population)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarize(
      share_mean = mean(prop),
      share_sd = sd(prop),
      share_n = n(),
      share_se = share_sd / sqrt(share_n),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |> 
    select(group, share_mean, share_se)


  ancestry <- results |>
    map(function(result) {
      result$persons |>
        filter(is.na(death_time)) |>
        left_join(result$ancestry, by = "person_id") |>
        group_by(group) |>
        summarize(ancestry_A = mean(group_A), ancestry_B = mean(group_B), .groups = "drop")
    }) |>
    bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarize(
      n = n(),
      ancestry_A_mean = mean(ancestry_A),
      ancestry_A_sd = sd(ancestry_A),
      ancestry_A_se = ancestry_A_sd / sqrt(n),
      ancestry_B_mean = mean(ancestry_B),
      ancestry_B_sd = sd(ancestry_B),
      ancestry_B_se = ancestry_B_sd / sqrt(n),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    select(group, ancestry_A_mean, ancestry_A_se, ancestry_B_mean, ancestry_B_se)

  full_join(share, ancestry, by = "group") |> mutate(scenario = scenario)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

df_inheritance <- df_inheritance |>
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      scenario, 
      levels = c("mother", "father", "random_parent", "same_sex",  "opposite_sex", "ancestry", 
                 "hierarchy_passing", "hierarchy_strict")
    )
  )
```

I have the following expectations by inheritance method:

- `mother`, `father`, `random_parent`, `same_sex`, and `opposite_sex` should all produce similar results with group size shares at the end that roughly match the start and similar ancestry shares where more A ancestry in group B than B ancestry in Group A.
- strict `hierarchy` (B > A) should cause the B group to grow relative to A. A individuals will have no B ancestry but B individuals will have more A ancestry than in other rules. I expect similar results with passing but the increase in B relative to A will be smaller  and A individuals will have a little B ancestry.
- I think ancestry based approach should favor the larger group A because over time their ancestry will dominate among mixed individuals and thus more mixed individuals will identify with A than B. B individuals will contain more A ancestry than vice verse.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ending-group-pop
#| fig-cap: Mean proportion of group B in final simulated population across inheritance scenarios, with 100 simulations per scenario. 95% confidence intervals shown. Dotted line shows the share B in the starting population.

start_share <- gweights["B"]/sum(gweights) 

df_inheritance |>
  filter(group == "B") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = scenario, y = share_mean))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = start_share, linetype = 2)+
  geom_point()+
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = share_mean - 1.96 * share_se, ymax = share_mean + 1.96 * share_se))+
  labs(y = "Proportion group B", x = NULL)+
  coord_flip()+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-ending-group-pop shows the mean proportion of the population belonging to group B at the end of each simulation by inheritance rule. The results show that all rules except the hierarchy case produce a group proportion consistent with the starting group share and the proportions are also statistically indistinguishable across those methods. The ancestry method does not shrink the size of the B group, contrary to expectation. 

The hierarchy rules produce a higher share of group B than the other methods and relative to the baseline, as expected. Strict hierarchy increases the B share more than hierarchy with some passing, also as expected. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-other-ancestry-share
#| fig-cap: Mean share of non-identifying ancestry for Group A and B individuals in the final simulated population across inheritance scenarios. 95% confidence intervals shown.

df_inheritance |>
  mutate(
    ancestry_other = if_else(group == "A", ancestry_B_mean, ancestry_A_mean),
    se = if_else(group == "A", ancestry_B_se, ancestry_A_se)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = scenario, y = ancestry_other, group = group, color = group))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = ancestry_other - 1.96 * se, ymax = ancestry_other + 1.96 * se))+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of ancestry from other group")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-other-ancestry-share shows the share of ancestry that each group has from the other group at the end of each simulation, meaned across all simulations. All methods except for ancestry and hierarchy produce the same shares within each group. As expected The proportion of A ancestry among B individuals is higher than the proportion of B ancestry among A individuals, because group A was a larger share of the starting population. 

For the ancestry method, the share of cross-group ancestry is higher for both groups than in all other methods except for the hierarchy results, but the larger increase is for group B, as expected. For the hierarchy method, strict hierarchy produces a 0% share of B ancestry among group A members because it is effectively a strict one-drop rule. The share of A ancestry among B individuals, on the other hand, is higher than for any other method because all mixed ancestry gets absorbed into group B. Hierarchy with some passing shows exactly the same pattern but with some slight moderation, as expected.

### Custom rules and mixed identities

To test out the custom rules and the emergence of mixed identities, I will use one of the multinomial logit models developed by Gullickson and Saperstein (2025) to assign births based on the share of A ancestry. This will only be applied to births whose parents differ in their own identities (otherwise assign the shared parental identity). The model will maximize the probability of identifying as AB at about 70% when the proportion of A ancestry is 50%. As that proportion moves toward either 0% or 100%, this probability will gradually decline and the probability of identifying with the dominant ancestry will increase.

I will run one simulation with an even group distribution between A and B at the start for 200 years using this custom inheritance model.

```{r}
#| label: run-custom-inheritance

# custom function
custom_inheritance <- create_group_inheritance(
  "custom",
  groups = c("A", "B", "AB"),
  fun = function(child_ancestry, mother_group, father_group, ...) {
    # Same identity or missing father: follow mother
    if (is.na(father_group) || mother_group == father_group) {
      return(mother_group)
    }

    # Entirely unknown ancestry: follow mother
    known <- 1 - child_ancestry[["unknown"]]
    if (known <= 0) return(mother_group)

    # if we are here then assign as a function of group A ancestry
    prop_A <- child_ancestry[["group_A"]] / known

    logits <- c(
      A  = -5.138 + 11.88 * prop_A - 15.3 * prop_A^2 + 9.553 * prop_A^3,
      B  = 0.949 - 9.39 * prop_A + 11.935 * prop_A^2 - 8.483 * prop_A^3,
      AB = 0
    )
    weights <- exp(logits - max(logits))

    sample(names(weights), size = 1, prob = weights)
  }
)

pop_baseline_custom <- create_baseline_population(50000, max_age = 100, 2000, group_weights = c("A" = 1, "B" = 1))

model_custom <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(pop_baseline_custom) |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates_usa2000) |>
  set_fertility(fertility_rates_overall_usa, inheritance = custom_inheritance) |>
  set_union_formation(
    "on_demand",
    matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(
      0, 5, group_exogamy = c("A:B" = -2.5, "A:AB" = -1.25, "B:AB" = -1.25)
    )
  )

result_custom <- simulate(model_custom, 200, seed = 42)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-group-share-custom-inheritance
#| fig-cap: Group share across time in custom inheritance simulation

result_custom |>
  calculate_population_size(2000:2200, by_group = TRUE) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  mutate(prop = population / sum(population)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop, group = group, fill = group))+
  geom_area()+
  labs(x = "year", y = "share of population")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-group-share-custom-inheritance shows the emergence of the mixed AB identity group over the simulation. Because the probability of mixed group identification is high, this population grows at the expense of both A and B. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-custom-inheritance-prob
#| fig-cap: Probability of group assignment as a function of proportion A ancestry among births to parents belonging to different groups for all births in a single simulation. Proportion A ancestry is plotted in 10 percent bins by the midpoint of the bin. 95% confidence intervals shown. The dotted line shows the expected probability from the inheritance model.

temp <- tibble(
  prop_A = seq(0.005, 0.995, 0.005),
  logit_A = -5.138 + 11.88 * prop_A - 15.3 * prop_A^2 + 9.553 * prop_A^3,
  logit_B = 0.949 - 9.39 * prop_A + 11.935 * prop_A^2 - 8.483 * prop_A^3,
  denom = exp(logit_A) + exp(logit_B) + exp(0),
  prob_A = exp(logit_A)/denom,
  prob_B = exp(logit_B)/denom,
  prob_AB = exp(0)/denom
) |>
  select(prop_A, starts_with("prob_")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("prob_"), names_prefix = "prob_", names_to = "group", values_to = "prop") |>
  rename(prop_a_group = prop_A)

result_custom$persons |>
  left_join(result_custom$ancestry, by = "person_id") |>
  left_join(
    result_custom$persons |> 
      select(person_id, group) |> 
      rename(father_id = person_id, group_father = group),
    by = "father_id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    result_custom$persons |> 
      select(person_id, group) |> 
      rename(mother_id = person_id, group_mother = group),
    by = "mother_id"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(group_father) & !is.na(group_mother) &
    group_father != group_mother) |>
  mutate(
    prop_a_group = cut(
      group_A,
      breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
      labels = FALSE,
      include.lowest = TRUE
    ) * 0.1 - 0.05
  ) |>
  group_by(prop_a_group, group) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n), se = sqrt(prop * (1 - prop) / sum(n))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop_a_group, y = prop, group = group, color = group))+
  geom_line(data = temp, linetype = 2)+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8)+
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = prop - 1.96 * se, ymax = prop + 1.96 * se), alpha = 0.8)+
  labs(x = "proportion A ancestry", y = "probability of group identity")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-custom-inheritance-prob shows the observed probability of being assigned to a given group as a function of share of A ancestry for births to parents from different groups. The dotted line shows the expected probabilities from the model. The results line up closely to expectation and most 95% confidence intervals contain the expected value.

## Speed Tests

Compare runtime and memory with and without groups, ancestry, and custom

```{r}
    }

    # Entirely unknown ancestry: follow mother
    known <- 1 - child_ancestry[["unknown"]]
    if (known <= 0) return(mother_group)
    
    # after all that just return randomly mother or father group
    sample(c(mother_group, father_group), 1)
  }
)


elapsed_time <- NULL
for(i in seq_along(1:nrow(scenarios))) {

  strat_method <- scenarios$strat_method[i]
  n_groups <- scenarios$n_groups[i]
  custom_inheritance <- scenarios$custom_inheritance[i]

  model <- hammel_model()

  if(!is.na(custom_inheritance) & custom_inheritance) {
    model_inheritance <- random_inheritance
  } else {
    model_inheritance <- "random_parent"
  }

  if (n_groups == 1) {
    model <- model |>
      set_population(population1) |>
      set_fertility(fertility_rates_overall_usa) |>
      set_mortality(mortality_rates_usa2000) |>
      set_union_formation("on_demand", matching1)
  } else if (n_groups == 2) {
    if (strat_method == "rate") {
      model <- model |> 
        set_population(population2) |>
        set_mortality(mortality_rates2) |>
        set_fertility(fertility_rates2, inheritance = model_inheritance) |>
        set_union_formation("on_demand", matching2)
    } else {
      model <- model |> 
        set_population(population2) |>
        set_mortality(mortality_rates_usa2000, group_prop_hazard = prop_hazards2) |>
        set_fertility(
          fertility_rates_overall_usa, 
          group_prop_hazard = prop_hazards2, 
          inheritance = model_inheritance
        ) |>
        set_union_formation("on_demand", matching2)
    }
  } else if (n_groups == 3) {
    if (strat_method == "rate") {
      model <- model |> 
        set_population(population3) |>
        set_mortality(mortality_rates3) |>
        set_fertility(fertility_rates3, inheritance = model_inheritance) |>
        set_union_formation("on_demand", matching3)
    } else {
      model <- model |> 
        set_population(population3) |>
        set_mortality(mortality_rates_usa2000, group_prop_hazard = prop_hazards3) |>
        set_fertility(
          fertility_rates_overall_usa, 
          group_prop_hazard = prop_hazards3,
          inheritance = model_inheritance
        ) |>
        set_union_formation("on_demand", matching3)
    }
  } else {
    if (strat_method == "rate") {
      model <- model |> 
        set_population(population4) |>
        set_mortality(mortality_rates4) |>
        set_fertility(fertility_rates4, inheritance = model_inheritance) |>
        set_union_formation("on_demand", matching4)
    } else {
      model <- model |> 
        set_population(population4) |>
        set_mortality(mortality_rates_usa2000, group_prop_hazard = prop_hazards4) |>
        set_fertility(
          fertility_rates_overall_usa, 
          group_prop_hazard = prop_hazards4,
          inheritance = model_inheritance
        ) |>
        set_union_formation("on_demand", matching4)
    }
  }


  timing <- system.time({result <- simulate(model, years = 100)})
  elapsed_time <- c(elapsed_time, unname(timing[["elapsed"]]))
  #cat(i)
}

scenarios$elapsed_time <- elapsed_time
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-time-tests
#| tbl-cap: Time (in seconds) to run simulations with differing parameters. All simulations start with 50,000 individuals and are simulated for 100 years.

scenarios |>
  mutate(strat_method = if_else(strat_method == "rate", "stratified rate", "proportional hazards")) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    strat_method ~ "Rate strat method",
    n_groups ~ "Number of groups",
    custom_inheritance ~ "Custom inheritance method",
    elapsed_time ~ "Time (in seconds)"
  ) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "-")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-tests
#| fig-cap: Time to run simulation by various factors. All simulations run for a 50K population over 100 years.

scenarios |>
  filter(n_groups > 1) |>
  mutate(strat_method = if_else(strat_method == "rate", "stratified rate", "proportional hazards")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_groups, y = elapsed_time, group = custom_inheritance, color = custom_inheritance))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  facet_wrap(~strat_method)+
  labs(x = "number of groups", y = "elapsed time in seconds", color = "custom inheritance")+
  theme_bw()
```


@tbl-time-tests and @fig-time-tests show the amount of time to process each simulation scenario. These numbers are not exact because other factors can affect total processing time. Adding groups in general increases processing time substantially. The single group simulation runs in about 0.28 seconds, while the two-group cases take at least five times as long. The slight curvature in the figure  suggests that computational time may increase faster than a linear progression with the number of groups. 

Using custom inheritance functions in R increased processing time, but the increase seems to be independent of the number of groups. The inheritance function used here was quite simple. More complex functions could increase time further.

The decision to use proportional hazards or stratified rates had no effect on computing time.
